context: that the white kitten had had nothing to do with it
simple: The white kitten was not part of it at all.
grammar: "had had" is the past perfect of "have": "had" is the helper and "had" is the main verb. "Have nothing to do with" means to have no part in something.

context: the ball of worsted Alice had been trying to wind up
simple: the ball of wool thread that Alice had been trying to wind up
grammar: "Alice had been trying..." is a relative clause with "that" left out: "the ball of worsted (that) Alice had been trying to wind up". It uses the past perfect continuous.

context: Suppose they had saved up all my punishments
simple: Think what would happen if they had kept all my punishments for later.
grammar: "Suppose + past perfect" means "What if...?" Alice asks about something that did not happen.

context: you never can tell, you know, unless our fire smokes
simple: You cannot know, unless our fire makes smoke.
grammar: "Unless" means "if not". "You never can tell" means that nobody can know.

context: I might have won, if it hadn’t been for that nasty Knight
simple: Perhaps I would have won, but the nasty Knight stopped me.
grammar: "If it hadn't been for X" means "without X". "Might have won" says it was possible, but it did not happen.

context: that she mightn’t take his breath away
simple: so that she would not take his breath away
grammar: "that she mightn't" means "so that she might not". It tells the purpose of lifting him slowly.

context: if I could get to the top of that hill
simple: I would see the garden much better if I could get to the top of that hill.
grammar: "if I could get..." talks about something Alice cannot do now. "I should see" tells what would happen if she could.

context: I could show you hills, in comparison with which you’d call that a valley
simple: I know of hills that are so high that you would call this one a valley.
grammar: "in comparison with which" means "when you put it next to them". "Which" stands for "hills" and joins this part to the word "hills".

context: I’ve heard nonsense, compared with which that would be as sensible as a dictionary
simple: I have heard nonsense that was so much worse that this would seem as sensible as a dictionary.
grammar: "compared with which" means "when you put it next to that". "Which" stands for "nonsense" and joins this part to the word "nonsense".

context: it takes all the running you can do, to keep in the same place
simple: You must run as much as you can, just to stay where you are.
grammar: "all the running you can do" means "as much running as you can do". "To keep in the same place" is an infinitive of purpose, meaning "in order to stay".

context: something about ‘horse’ and ‘hoarse,’ you know
simple: You could make a joke about the words "horse" and "hoarse", you know.
grammar: Wordplay: "horse" and "hoarse" are spelled differently but sound the same. Just before, the voice was hoarse, and Alice thought it sounded like a horse.

context: if the governess wanted to call you to your lessons
simple: For example, if the teacher wanted to call you to your lessons
grammar: "If + past tense" ("wanted") with "would" in the next part ("she would call out") is a conditional that talks about something that is only imagined.

context: the governess would never think of excusing me lessons for that
simple: The teacher would never think of letting me miss lessons because of that.
grammar: "excuse me lessons" means "let me off lessons": the verb "excuse" has two objects, "me" and "lessons".

context: of course you’d miss your lessons
simple: Of course, you would not go to your lessons.
grammar: Wordplay: "Miss" (the word the governess calls) and "miss" (to not go to something) sound the same. The Gnat then says, "That's a joke."

context: Waxworks weren’t made to be looked at for nothing, nohow!
simple: People did not make waxworks so that you could look at them without paying.
grammar: "for nothing" means "without paying". "Nohow" is a non-standard word for "not at all", so the sentence has a double negative, with "weren't" and "nohow".

context: if it were so, it would be; but as it isn’t, it ain’t
simple: If it were so, it would be so. But because it is not so, it is not.
grammar: "If it were so, it would be" is a conditional with "were" for an unreal idea. "Ain't" is a spoken short form of "isn't".

context: so that the Carpenter couldn’t count how many he took
simple: He did this so that the Carpenter could not count the number he took.
grammar: "so that" begins a clause of purpose. It says why the Walrus held his handkerchief in front.

context: If I wasn’t real,” Alice said —half-laughing through her tears
simple: Alice said, half laughing through her tears: if I were not real, I would not be able to cry.
grammar: "If I wasn't real" is an idea that is not true: Alice says she is real. The main part comes after the words "Alice said": "I shouldn't be able to cry".

context: shouldn’t have minded it so much,” said Tweedledum, “if it hadn’t been
simple: I would not have minded so much if it had not been a new one.
grammar: "shouldn't have minded... if it hadn't been" is a past conditional: it talks about something that did not happen in the past. "Hadn't been" means "had not been".

context: Well, yes, if you call that a-dressing
simple: Yes, if you want to call that "a-dressing".
grammar: Wordplay: Alice said "addressing" (speaking to someone), but the Queen hears "a-dressing", which sounds the same. Her next words are about dressing herself.

context: You couldn’t have it if you did want it
simple: You could not have it even if you wanted it.
grammar: "if you did want it": "did" is a stress word that makes "want" stronger. "Couldn't have" here means you would not be allowed to have it.

context: there’s one great advantage in it, that one’s memory works both ways
simple: There is one big good point: a person's memory works forwards and backwards.
grammar: "One's" means "a person's" and is a formal way to talk about people in general. The "that" clause tells what the advantage is.

context: it wouldn’t be all the better his being punished
simple: It would not be better if he were punished.
grammar: "his being punished" is a phrase with a possessive ("his") before an "-ing" word. It means "that he is punished". "All the better" means "even better".

context: The egg seems to get further away the more I walk towards it
simple: The more I walk towards the egg, the further away it seems to get.
grammar: "the more I walk" means "as I walk more". Two things change together: more walking, more distance.

context: If I’d meant that, I’d have said it
simple: If I had meant that, I would have said it.
grammar: "I'd" is short for "I had" in the first part and "I would" in the second. It is a past conditional about something that did not happen.

context: One can’t, perhaps,” said Humpty Dumpty, “but two can
simple: One person cannot, perhaps, but two people can.
grammar: "but two can" leaves out words, as "but two can help it". Humpty Dumpty means that with help from another person you could have left off at seven.

context: it means just what I choose it to mean
simple: It means exactly the thing that I choose it to mean.
grammar: "just what I choose it to mean" is a noun clause: "what" means "the thing which". "Neither more nor less" follows and means exactly that.

context: I only wish I had such eyes,” the King remarked
simple: I wish I had such eyes, but I do not.
grammar: "wish + past tense" ("had") talks about something that is not true now.

context: You might as well try to stop a Bandersnatch
simple: Trying to stop a minute is as hopeless as trying to stop a Bandersnatch.
grammar: "You might as well try to..." says that something is as hopeless as the thing named. Here the King says that stopping a minute is as hard as stopping a Bandersnatch.

context: it’s as well to be provided for everything
simple: It is wise to be ready for everything.
grammar: "it's as well to" means "it is wise to". "Provided for" means "made ready for".

context: To guard against the bites of sharks
simple: They are to keep the horse safe from shark bites.
grammar: This is an infinitive of purpose with no subject. It answers Alice's question "What are they for?" and "guard against" means "keep safe from".

context: the more head downwards I am, the more I keep inventing new things
simple: When my head is lower, I think of more new things.
grammar: "the more..., the more..." shows that two things grow together: more upside down, more new things.

context: I was as fast as —as lightning, you know
simple: I was as fast as lightning, you know. Here "fast" means held in place, not quick.
grammar: Wordplay on "fast": it can mean held in place, or very quick. The Knight was stuck in the helmet, but "as fast as lightning" usually means very quick. Alice says it is a different kind of fastness.

context: That’s what the name is called. The name really is ‘The Aged Aged Man.’
simple: That is what the name is called. The name itself is "The Aged Aged Man".
grammar: The Knight separates "what the name is called" from "what the name really is". The song has four different names in this part.

context: And the sooner we begin it, the better
simple: If we begin sooner, it will be better.
grammar: "the sooner..., the better" is a pattern with "the" and a word like "sooner" or "better". It shows that two things change together: sooner is better.

context: What do you suppose is the use of a child without any meaning
simple: What use do you think a child is without any meaning?
grammar: "do you suppose" is put into the question "What is the use of...?". After it, the word order is like a statement: "is the use", with no "does".

context: I said you couldn’t if you tried
simple: I said that you could not deny it, even if you tried.
grammar: "you couldn't" leaves out "deny it", which comes from the sentence before. The Red Queen answers Alice's "I don't deny things with my hands".

context: I speaks English, doesn’t I?
simple: I speak English, do I not?
grammar: The Frog uses non-standard grammar: "I speaks" and "doesn't I" use the third-person verb forms with "I". The standard forms are "I speak" and "don't I".

context: I’ll shake you into a kitten, that I will
simple: I will shake you until you are a kitten, I really will.
grammar: "that I will" is added at the end for emphasis: it repeats "I will" to show that Alice means what she says.

context: it must have been either me or the Red King
simple: I am sure it was either me or the Red King.
grammar: "must have been" shows that Alice is sure about something in the past. "Either... or" gives two possible answers.
